rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage from 96:9 onward recounts some consequences of human tyranny and threatens the one who prevents prayer.
rows.anchor: ذكر لبعض آثار الطغيان ووعيد عليها

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that Abū Jahl swore by al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā to trample the Prophet, then retreated from a fiery trench, terror, and wings; the Prophet said angels would seize him limb by limb. This occasioned 96:6 through the sūra’s end.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة أن أبا جهل حلف باللات والعزى

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies the prohibitor as Umayya b. Khalaf and the worshipper as Salmān; al-Ālūsī says this report is unsound because Salmān became Muslim in Medina while the sūra is Meccan.
rows.anchor: وقول الحسن هو أمية بن خلف كان ينهى سلمان عن الصلاة لا يكاد يصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra is Meccan and Salmān became Muslim after the Hijra; if Umayya’s reported action occurred, the verse’s general threat would include him.
rows.anchor: فإن كان ما حكي عن أمية واقعاً فحكمها شامل له

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān reports that the prayer referred to was the noon prayer.
rows.anchor: على ما حكى أبو حيان صلاة الظهر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account says this was a congregational prayer, the first congregation in Islam, with Abū Bakr and ʿAlī; Abū Ṭālib passed with Jaʿfar and urged him to join his cousin.
rows.anchor: وحكي أيضاً أنها كانت تصلي جماعة وهي أول جماعة أقيمت في الإسلام

rows.speaker: أبو طالب
rows.claim: Abū Ṭālib’s cited poem calls ʿAlī and Jaʿfar his trusted support in hardship, says kin will not abandon the Prophet, and urges them to defend their cousin.
rows.anchor: والله لا أخذ النبي ولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer was instituted on the night of the Isrāʾ by consensus; Ibn Ḥazm specifically claims consensus that this was one year before the Hijra.
rows.anchor: وادعى ابن حزم الإجماع على أنه كان قبل الهجرة بسنة

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Fāris dates the Isrāʾ to one year and three months before the Hijra.
rows.anchor: وجزم ابن فارس بأنه كان قبلها بسنة وثلاثة أشهر

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī dates the Isrāʾ to one year and five months before the Hijra.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي بسنة وخمسة أشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The congregational-prayer account involving Abū Ṭālib conflicts with the chronology: he died about three years before the Hijra, before prayer was prescribed.
rows.anchor: وموت أبي طالب كان قبل الهجرة بنحو ثلاث سنين

rows.speaker: القاضي عياض
rows.claim: Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ transmits al-Zuhrī’s view, preferred by al-Nawawī and al-Qurṭubī, that the Isrāʾ occurred five years after the prophetic commission; al-Ālūsī notes objections to it.
rows.anchor: حكى القاضي عياض عن الزهري ورجحه النووي والقرطبي أن الإسراء كان بعد البعث بخمس سنين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The word for forbidding is explained as preventing; its use hints that the tyrant could do no more than this, though other reports show verbal prohibition.
rows.anchor: والنهي قيل بمعنى المنع وعبر به إشارة إلى عدم اقتدار اللعين على غير ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Abū Jahl came while the Prophet prayed and repeatedly challenged him, “Did I not forbid you?” Al-Tirmidhī authenticated this report.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال «كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يصلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future-form wording evokes the past scene as something strange and astonishing.
rows.anchor: والتعبير بما يفيد الاستقبال لاستحضار الصورة الماضية لنوع غرابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here raʾayta means “tell me”: since seeing leads to knowledge, asking about seeing functions as asking about its object; grammarians have two analyses of this usage.
rows.anchor: والمراد من أرأيت أخبرني فإن الرؤية لما كانت سبباً للعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the principal parse, the first raʾayta takes the relative clause as its first object; the second and third have an omitted first object referring back, and the third’s second object is “does he not know that God sees?”
rows.anchor: والمفعول الأول للأول الموصول وللثاني والثالث محذوف وهو ضمير يعود عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent ellipsis here is semantic request, not tanāzuʿ: clauses cannot be elided as competing syntactic governors; al-Ālūsī illustrates with a report about Zayd.
rows.anchor: وليس ذلك من التنازع لأن الجمل لا يصح إضمارها وإنما هو من الطلب المعنوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answers to both conditional clauses are omitted, with 96:14 indicating them; another parse takes raʾayta itself to point to the answer soon to be stated.
rows.anchor: وجواب الشرط في الجملتين محذوف لدلالة ألم يعلم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address in all three questions may be to anyone capable of understanding; another view takes it as addressing humankind, as in “to your Lord” at 96:8.
rows.anchor: والخطاب في الكل على ما اختاره جمع لكل من يصلح أن يكون مخاطباً

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take the indefinite accusative ʿabdan at face value as indefiniteness.
rows.anchor: وتنوين { عبداً } على ما هو ظاهر كلام البعض للتنكير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī also prefers reading the indefinite as magnifying the Prophet, the audacity of the prohibition, and the astonishment it deserves.
rows.anchor: والتنوين في عبداً لتفخيمه عليه الصلاة والسلام واستعظام النهي وتأكيد التعجيب منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restricting the prohibition with the temporal clause suggests that the prohibition occurred while the person was engaged in prayer.
rows.anchor: وتقييد النهي بالظرف يشعر بأن النهي عن الصلاة حال التلبس بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clauses are separated to intensify censure and threat, presenting each as independently deserving condemnation.
rows.anchor: وفصل بين الجمل للاعتناء بأمر التشنيع والوعيد حيث أشعر أن كل جملة مقصودة على حيالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage escalates: first it condemns forbidding prayer without regard to the forbidding person’s supposed status, then condemns it if he claims guidance, then if he actually denies prayer’s truth and turns away.
rows.anchor: والحاصل أنه تعالى شنع وأوعد على النهي عن الصلاة بدون تعرض لحال الناهي الزعمي أو الحقيقي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority do not limit the conditionals as al-Ālūsī did: the first supposes guidance or enjoining piety as claimed, the second denial and turning away as the commentators affirm.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على عدم تقييد ما في حيز الشرطيتين بما ذكرنا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: For the majority, the conditional form feigns latitude and taunts: there can be no guidance in forbidding worship of God and ordering idol worship, while the denier plainly is astray; both conditions return to one point.
rows.anchor: إذ لا يكون في النهي عن عبادته تعالى والأمر بعبادة الأصنام هدى البتة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One parse makes the first raʾayta visual, needing no second object, and the second and third cognitive, with their conditional clauses and answers filling the second-object position.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن الرؤية في الجملة الأولى بصرية فلا تحتاج إلى مفعول ثان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another parse treats all three as cognitive: the first takes the relative clause as object one, its condition as object two, and the third omits object one while explicitly supplying the threatening answer.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن أرأيت في الجمل الثلاث من الرؤية القلبية والمفعول الأول للأولى الموصول

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: In that parse, the final clause is unjoined to reinforce the rebuke and signal the condition’s truth; stating its answer makes the threat explicit, while the first conditional’s answer is understood from the second.
rows.anchor: وفي الإتيان بالجملة الأخيرة من دون العطف ترشيح للكلام المبكت وتنبيه على حقية الشرط

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further parse makes the second and third raʾayta repetitions of the first; both conditionals fill its second-object slot, 96:14 answers the second, and the first answer is omitted by analogy.
rows.anchor: وقيل أرأيت في الجملتين الثانية والثالثة تكرار للأولى

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān objects that an interrogative sentence cannot answer a conditional without faʾ; he says grammarians require it whenever the answer expresses a request, except in poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان إن وقوع جملة الاستفهام جواباً للشرط بغير فاء لا أعلم أحد أجازه

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān and others object that raʾayta’s second object must be an interrogative or oath clause; al-Khafājī answers that the condition and question together can fill that slot.
rows.anchor: إلا جملة استفهامية كمانص عليه أبو حيان وجماعة أو قسمية

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī says the conditional and its interrogative answer may be taken literally together as raʾayta’s second object, or treated as filling it together because they jointly indicate that object; al-Raḍī and al-Damāmīnī also state this.
rows.anchor: وقال الخفاجي إن جعل الشرطية في موقع المفعول والجملة الاستفهامية في موقع جواب الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibitor and worshipper are outside the addressee role in the immediate context; al-Baḥr prefers addressing the Prophet, while another permits addressing the unbelieving prohibitor in a generic scene.
rows.anchor: ولم يجعلوا فيما ذكر الخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ولا للكافر الناهي

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ assigns “was” and “commanded” to the praying servant, but “denied,” “turned away,” and “knows” to the prohibitor; the implied conclusion is how astonishing the case is.
rows.anchor: وحاصل المعنى على ما قال الفراء أرأيت الذي ينهى عبداً يصلي والمنهي على الهدى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another proposal shifts the second question’s addressee to the disbeliever and the third’s to the Prophet, like a judge addressing two litigants; its “or” is division equivalent to “and.”
rows.anchor: فهو عز وجل كالحاكم الذي حضر الخصمان يخاطب هذا مرة والآخر أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second conditional mentions enjoining piety because the prohibition concerned prayer and its opposite; the phrase may have been omitted from the first conditional for brevity and supplied here.
rows.anchor: ولعل ذكر الأمر بالتقوى في الجملة الثانية لأن النهي على ما قيل كان عن الصلاة والأمر بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer is named before verbal enjoining because it is an active call, stronger than speech; an exemplar’s action effectively says, “Do this.”
rows.anchor: واقتصر على ذكر الصلاة ولم يعكس لأن الأمر بالتقوى دعوة قولية والصلاة دعوة فعلية والفعل أقوى من القول

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A different view says the first clause describes forbidding someone during prayer, not necessarily forbidding prayer itself; since prayer both perfects the worshipper and calls others, the prohibition may target both.
rows.anchor: وعامة أحوال الصلاة لما انحصرت في تكميل أنفس المصلي بالعبادة وتكميل غيره بالدعوة

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam reads the condition as asking whether a sensible, wealthy man would not do better to seek guidance and command piety than disbelieve and prohibit worship; God laments his forfeiture of high ranks for low ones.
rows.anchor: وجوز الإمام كون الخطاب في الكل له عليه الصلاة والسلام وقال في بيان معنى

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: ʿIṣām al-Dīn reads 96:9 as tyranny born of self-sufficiency, 96:11–12 as rebuke for forfeiting guidance and piety, and 96:13 as rebuke for earning punishment and distance from God; 96:14 is a severe threat.
rows.anchor: واعتبر عصام الدين هذه الجملة توبيخاً على تفويت ما ينفع وما بعدها توبيخاً على كسب ما يضر

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: For ʿIṣām al-Dīn, the opening question testifies to tyranny: the self-sufficient person goes beyond ingratitude and makes the servant sent to stop it commit ingratitude.
rows.anchor: عصام الدين هذه الجملة توبيخاً على تفويت ما ينفع وما بعدها توبيخاً على كسب ما يضر

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: ʿIṣām al-Dīn takes the second question as rebuking lost benefit: what victory the man would have gained had he followed guidance or enjoined piety.
rows.anchor: عصام الدين هذه الجملة توبيخاً على تفويت ما ينفع وما بعدها توبيخاً على كسب ما يضر

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: ʿIṣām al-Dīn takes the final question as rebuke for earned harm: denial and turning away merit punishment and distance from the Lord, followed by a severe threat.
rows.anchor: عصام الدين هذه الجملة توبيخاً على تفويت ما ينفع وما بعدها توبيخاً على كسب ما يضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī calls ʿIṣām al-Dīn’s overall reading far-fetched and leaves the intent to God after reviewing the preceding analyses.
rows.anchor: وهو كما ترى فتأمل جميع ما تقدم والله تعالى بمراده أعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although revealed about Abū Jahl, the threat applies to everyone who prohibits prayer; this does not forbid objecting to prayer in usurped places or disliked times, since the objection concerns a concomitant quality, not prayer itself.
rows.anchor: ثم إن الآية وإن نزلت في أبي جهل عليه اللعنة لكن كل من نهى عن الصلاة ومنع منها فهو شريكه في الوعيد

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī, seeing people pray before the Eid prayer, said he had not seen the Prophet do so; asked why he did not forbid them, he feared the threat, or said he preferred to teach what he had seen rather than forbid a worshipper.
rows.anchor: فروي عن أمير المؤمنين كرم الله تعالى وجهه أنه رأى في المصلي أقواماً يصلون قبل صلاة العيد

rows.speaker: أبو يوسف
rows.claim: Abū Yūsuf asked Abū Ḥanīfa whether a worshipper should say “My Lord, forgive me” while rising from bowing; Abū Ḥanīfa prescribed the praise formula and prostration without explicitly forbidding it.
rows.anchor: فقد روي أن أبا يوسف قال له أيقول المصلي حين يرفع رأسه من الركوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By analogy, the caution applies to prohibiting other forms of worship; there is no difference between verbal and situational prohibition, including distracting someone from worship, a widespread practice.
rows.anchor: ويقاس على النهي عن الصلاة النهي عن غيرها من أنواع العبادة ولا فرق بين النهي القالي والنهي الحالي
